screens.title: The Power of Documentation
screens.narratorSegment: Documentation is a tool, not a trophy. In this lesson we'll adopt a pragmatic view: write what adds value, keep it close to the code when possible, and remove or refactor what becomes a liability. You will learn to apply the DRY principle to documentation, choose the right type of document for the job, and use living documentation so facts and behavior stay synchronized with code. We'll look at examples ranging from README files and lightweight docstrings to OpenAPI machine-readable specifications and executable specifications used as tests. I will also point out common traps that create documentation rot, and practical ways to recover a project that has accumulated stale artifacts. By the end you'll be able to judge whether a document should exist, where its single authoritative source should live, and how to keep it accurate with minimal ongoing cost. Think of documentation as ongoing code hygiene: do only what preserves clarity and reduces future friction. Which part of your next task could benefit most from a living document?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › The Power of Documentation
The Power of Documentation
When and how to document effectively so your work remains useful and maintainable.
Documentation should maximize clarity and knowledge transfer while minimizing maintenance cost. Use code as the primary source where possible, create living API specs, and document high-level decisions that cannot live in code. If a document does not add value, treat it like dead code: refactor or remove it.
In this lesson
DRY for docs, living specs, README best-practices, code comments that explain why, and avoiding documentation rot.
Why it matters
Good documentation reduces onboarding time, avoids costly misunderstandings, and keeps design knowledge available for future changes.
Visual concept
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Code as single source
Prefer generated docs and self-documenting code.
Living specs
Executable specifications keep docs truthful.
Minimal READMEs
Practical setup and usage examples are enough.
Explore Key Topics
DRY for Documentation
Keep one authoritative source for each fact or behavior.
Living Documentation
Use specifications and tests that execute as verification of docs.
Readable READMEs
Practical setup, examples, and how to view generated docs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to make pragmatic decisions about when to create documentation and how to keep it accurate with minimal effort. You will articulate a philosophy of "just enough" and "just in time" documentation and identify the appropriate place for architectural notes, A P I specs, user guides, code comments, and READMEs. You will apply the DRY principle to documentation, ensuring each fact has a single authoritative home, and you will be able to convert static artifacts into living documentation when appropriate. Finally, you will recognize common pitfalls such as documentation rot and excessive, obvious commenting, and you will apply corrective strategies such as generating docs from code or turning requirements into executable specifications. These skills reduce maintenance overhead, improve onboarding, and preserve institutional knowledge. Picture deciding whether a team needs a short architecture note or a generated OpenAPI file and choosing the option that will stay accurate over time.

screens.title: Pragmatic Documentation Philosophy
screens.narratorSegment: Pragmatic documentation is a deliberate practice: create only what helps someone understand or act, and store it where it will be maintained. This means distinguishing between information that is best expressed in code, and information that requires external prose. For example, naming a function clearly keeps its intended behavior visible; that is code-level documentation. High-level design decisions, trade-offs, or business rules often cannot be encoded directly and belong in a concise architectural note. The practical consequence is that every piece of information should have one authoritative home. Apply the DRY principle by avoiding duplicates across code comments, wikis, and long design documents. When duplication exists, divergence inevitably follows. A common misconception is that more documentation always reduces risk. In fact, excessive and redundant documentation increases risk because it becomes stale and misleading. A better habit is to write what is essential, keep it short, and treat documentation like code: review it, refactor it, and delete it when it is no longer useful. Consider the decision of whether to write a ten-page design doc or a one-page architecture note with an OpenAPI spec. The one-page note paired with an executable spec will usually be easier to maintain and more trustworthy. What single fact in your current project should move to a single authoritative source?

keyIdea.title: Document intentionally
keyIdea.text: Create concise, maintained artifacts and prefer code or machine-readable specs as the authoritative source when possible.

content.html:
Core Concept › Pragmatic Documentation Philosophy
Definition and principles
Document just enough, store facts in one place, and keep docs maintained like code.
DRY for docs: single authoritative source for each fact or behavior.
Living docs: tie documentation to code or tests to avoid drift.
Triage regularly: review, refactor, or remove stale documents.
Key Takeaway

Fewer, authoritative documents maintained close to implementation are more useful than many stale artifacts.

Concrete example
Compare a 50-page design PDF that is never updated with a one-page architecture note and an OpenAPI file generated from code.
Scenario:
  • Long design PDF: details duplicate code and quickly diverge.
  • One-page note + OpenAPI: the note explains trade-offs, OpenAPI is generated and accurate.
  • Outcome: team trusts the generated docs and reviews the note as part of changes.
Common misconception: more text equals better clarity. Reality: redundancy breeds inconsistency and distrust.

screens.title: DRY for Documentation
screens.narratorSegment: Applying DRY to documentation is a step-by-step process you can use on any project. First, identify facts that are repeated across code, comments, and external docs. These are the places where divergence will happen. Second, select the single authoritative home for each fact. If the fact is operational or A P I-shaped, put it in a machine-readable specification such as OpenAPI. If it is an implementation detail that is best expressed in code, prefer self-documenting names and minimal comments that explain intent, not mechanics. Third, remove duplicates and link to the authoritative source. Replace pasted examples with a small pointer or a generated snippet. Fourth, enforce the authority with automation: generate docs from the source, run tests that validate behavior, or include doc review in code review. A common mistake is to centralize the wrong thing — for example, placing high-level architectural rationale in auto-generated files where it will be lost. Keep rationale in human-authored notes and keep procedural facts in generated specs. As an exercise, take a README and a set of code comments, identify one duplicated claim, choose its authoritative source, and remove the other occurrences. How will your chosen authority be maintained going forward?

keyIdea.title: DRY steps
keyIdea.text: Find duplicates, pick an authoritative source, remove copies, and automate validation to prevent divergence.

content.html:
Process Flow › DRY for Documentation
DRY process
1
Discover duplicates
Audit wikis, READMEs, comments, and code for repeated facts.
2
Choose authority
Pick code, OpenAPI, or a short architecture note depending on the fact.
3
Remove duplicates
Replace extra copies with links or generated content.
4
Automate checks
Generate docs, add tests, and include doc review in pull requests.
Misconception check: Centralizing everything in generated files removes human context. Keep rationale in short notes while moving concrete facts into generated specs.
Example
A date format rule appears in code comments, API docs, and a wiki. Make OpenAPI the authoritative source for the API contract, remove the wiki copy, and add a link to the OpenAPI file from the wiki.
Try this:
  1. Find one repeated property across docs and code.
  2. Decide if it belongs in code, OpenAPI, or a note.
  3. Replace duplicates with a link or generated snippet and record the authority.

screens.title: Types of Documentation
screens.narratorSegment: Different documentation types serve distinct audiences and purposes, and choosing the right one matters. Architectural documentation communicates high-level structure, major components, and design decisions. It is valuable for engineers making strategic changes and for new team members. A P I documentation describes how to interact with a service, often including endpoints, payload shapes, authentication, and error codes; when machine-readable it becomes living documentation. User documentation addresses end-user needs and is typically produced by product or documentation teams. Code comments should be used sparingly to explain why code exists or to note non-obvious constraints, not to restate the code's mechanics. A README is the project's front door: a short explanation, setup instructions, and a simple usage example. A common mistake is treating one long document as a catch-all. For example, burying A P I contract details inside a lengthy architecture doc reduces discoverability for A P I consumers. Instead, place each concern where the appropriate consumer will look and make links between them. To practice, pick a small project and list which facts belong in each document type and why. Which of those facts can be generated from code so they remain accurate?

keyIdea.text: Put architecture rationale in notes, API contracts in specs, usage in READMEs, and intent in minimal code comments.

content.html:
Comparison › Types of Documentation
Purpose & Audience
Architectural Documentation
High-level structure and design rationale for engineers and architects.
API Documentation
Contracts, payloads, and error codes for API consumers; ideal when machine-readable.
User Documentation
Guides and how-tos for end users or product teams.
Code Comments
Explain intent or surprising constraints, not obvious behavior.
README
Setup, run instructions, and a quick example for new contributors.
Concrete scenario
A public API needs consumer-facing docs and internal architecture notes. Keep the API contract in OpenAPI, write a short README with usage examples and a link to the generated interactive docs, and place rationale for design choices in a concise architecture note.
Practice prompt:
  • List three facts about your project.
  • Assign each fact to architecture note, OpenAPI, README, or code comment.
  • Decide which facts can be generated from code and mark them.

screens.title: Docstrings and Code Comments
screens.narratorSegment: Docstrings and comments are often misused to state the obvious. The pragmatic rule is simple: prefer self-documenting code for the what, and use comments to explain intent, constraints, and rationale. A good docstring briefly states the function's purpose, parameters, return values, and important edge cases that the code alone does not express. In the provided factorial example, the docstring explains the mathematical intent, the meaning of parameters, and the exceptions raised for invalid input. That docstring adds value because the algorithm is simple but the contract and error behavior need to be explicit. Comments on a route or A P I should describe the purpose of the endpoint, not repeat the request parsing logic. A common misconception is that every line requires a comment; instead, review code to see whether a clearer name or small refactor makes a comment unnecessary. When you must comment, keep it high-level and stable. Practice by opening a small function you wrote recently and asking: does this comment explain why or just restate the code? If it restates, remove or replace it with a clearer name. Which comment in your codebase explains an important trade-off?

keyIdea.title: Comment intent, not mechanics
keyIdea.text: Docstrings should state intent, parameters, and constraints; comments should explain why a decision was made.

content.html:
Definition › Docstrings and Code Comments
Guidelines
  • Prefer clear names and small functions to commenting the obvious.
  • Use docstrings for purpose, parameters, return values, and exceptions.
  • Keep comments focused on rationale and non-obvious constraints.
Misconception: Comments prevent bugs. Reality: stale comments mislead; tests and clear code prevent bugs more reliably.
Concrete example
A concise docstring for a factorial function explains intent, parameter constraints, and raises behavior.
# app.py - docstring example
def factorial(n):
    """
    Calculates the factorial of a non-negative integer.

    This function computes n! for a given integer n.
    It returns 1 for n=0 and raises for invalid input.

    :param n: An integer for which to calculate the factorial.
    :type n: int
    :raises ValueError: If n is a negative integer.
    :returns: The factorial of n.
    :rtype: int
    """
    if not isinstance(n, int):
        raise TypeError("Input must be an integer.")
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("Factorial is not defined for negative numbers.")
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    result = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        result *= i
    return result
Exercise: Open a function, find any comment that repeats its code, and replace it with a clearer name or a short docstring that explains intent.

screens.title: Making API Docs Living with OpenAPI
screens.narratorSegment: An OpenAPI file is documentation and source of truth in a single machine-readable artifact. By describing endpoints, request and response schemas, authentication, and error conditions in OpenAPI, you can generate interactive documentation that matches the server behavior. The YAML spec shown in this chapter for a create-user endpoint is itself the documentation. Tools will render it and keep it discoverable for A P I consumers. The pragmatic benefit is that the spec can be generated from annotations in code or act as a contract validated by tests, reducing documentation rot. A common mistake is keeping a separate Word document with parameter lists; that quickly diverges. Instead, author or generate the OpenAPI spec, include it in the repository, and point your README to the generated interactive docs. As a concrete practice, when you change an endpoint, update the spec as part of the same change or keep tests that assert the spec and implementation agree. This keeps consumers and developers aligned and reduces the drift that causes bugs and support load. Making API Docs Living with OpenAPI means use openapi for machine-readable api contracts and generate interactive docs so the spec remains authoritative and discoverable.. In practical terms, an openapi spec as the authoritative api contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: OpenAPI = living contract
keyIdea.text: Use OpenAPI for machine-readable API contracts and generate interactive docs so the spec remains authoritative and discoverable.

content.html:
Process Flow › OpenAPI as Living Documentation
Why OpenAPI helps
  • Defines endpoints and payloads in a machine-readable format.
  • Generates interactive docs that API consumers can test.
  • Can be generated from code annotations to remain accurate.
Misconception: A spec removes the need for tests. Reality: tests should validate the implementation against the spec.
Example OpenAPI fragment
paths:
  /users:
    post:
      summary: Create a new user
      description: Registers a new user with the system.
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              required:
                - username
                - email
                - password
              properties:
                username:
                  type: string
                  description: Unique username for the new user.
                email:
                  type: string
                  format: email
                  description: User's email address.
                password:
                  type: string
                  format: password
                  description: User's password (min 8 chars, incl. special char).
      responses:
        '201':
          description: User created successfully.
        '400':
          description: Invalid input.
        '409':
          description: Username or email already exists.
Practice: Keep the OpenAPI spec in the repository and update it in the same change as code that modifies endpoints.

screens.title: Architectural Documentation That Ages Well
screens.narratorSegment: Architectural documentation should capture the significant choices that future engineers need to understand the system, not a line-by-line recreation of code. Focus on components, interactions, and the rationale for major trade-offs. Use diagrams sparingly and pair them with short prose explaining why choices were made. The goal is to reduce surprise when someone modifies a subsystem, so include the constraints and assumptions that would be easy to overlook. A common error is to document every technical detail; that becomes a maintenance burden. Instead, write concise architecture notes that point to code for the details and include links to generated A P I specs for contractual information. Maintain these notes in the repository and review them in design reviews. For practice, identify a design choice in your codebase, explain the trade-offs in one paragraph, and store that paragraph in a short architecture note. Will the next engineer be able to understand the reason behind that choice quickly? Architectural Documentation That Ages Well means architectural notes should explain trade-offs and constraints, not replicate implementation details.. In practical terms, capture key decisions and trade-offs, not every detail. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Document rationale
keyIdea.text: Architectural notes should explain trade-offs and constraints, not replicate implementation details.

content.html:
Architecture › Notes that age well
What to capture
  • Major components and responsibilities.
  • Key interactions and boundaries.
  • Critical constraints and why trade-offs were chosen.
Avoid low-level code duplication; link to source code and generated API specs for details.
Example note
One paragraph explaining a choice to use eventual consistency for a service, including the trade-offs and the constraints that required that decision.
Practice prompt:
  1. Pick a subsystem with a non-obvious design choice.
  2. Write a one-paragraph rationale: the constraint, the alternatives, and why the current approach was chosen.
  3. Store that paragraph in the repository as a short architecture note and link to code and tests.

screens.title: Executable Specifications and Living Documentation
screens.narratorSegment: Executable specifications are documentation expressed in a form that can be run as tests. When specifications are executable, documentation rot is prevented because mismatches between docs and behavior cause failures that require correction. Behavior-Driven Development frameworks allow you to write human-readable scenarios that double as tests. The Pragmatic approach asks you to use living documentation where possible for behavior that matters to consumers. For APIs, combining an OpenAPI contract with tests that exercise the endpoints is a strong pattern. For business rules, a short set of executable scenarios can serve both as documentation and verification. A misconception is that executable specs require heavy tooling and slow development. In practice, start small: pick a few critical behaviors and codify them. If an outdated document caused a bug before, turning that case into an executable spec both documents the expected behavior and prevents regression. What behavior in your project would you capture as an executable spec first? Executable Specifications and Living Documentation means make crucial behavior executable so documentation is validated by tests and cannot silently drift.. In practical terms, use tests and human-readable specs to keep documentation truthful. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Doc Triage and Maintenance
screens.narratorSegment: Documentation triage is a practical rhythm for keeping artifacts useful. Start by cataloging existing documents and noting when they were last updated. For each document ask three questions: does it still reflect the system's behavior, who uses it, and can the information be moved to a single authoritative source? If the answer is no, either update it, convert it into a generated spec, or delete it. Include doc changes in code reviews and add simple tests or checks that alert when the authoritative source and implementation diverge. A common pitfall is assigning triage to a single person without integrating it into the team's workflow. Triage works best when it's part of the development lifecycle: make documentation updates part of the definition of done and enforce them in pull requests. For practice, pick one stale document, decide whether to update, generate, or delete it, and record your decision and the authoritative source. Triage checklist

screens.title: What Causes Documentation Rot and How to Recover
screens.narratorSegment: Documentation rot happens when documents and implementation diverge. Symptoms include outdated parameter lists, inaccurate examples, or contradictory comments. Root causes are duplicated information, lack of ownership, and no automation tying docs to code. To recover, start with triage: find the most dangerous inaccuracies and correct them first. Replace duplicated facts with a single authoritative source and add automated checks or tests where feasible. If a document is low value and high maintenance, delete it. Treat documentation changes like code: include them in pull requests and test suites. A common recovery mistake is trying to update everything at once. Instead, prioritize by risk and act where stale docs cause incorrect behavior or onboarding friction. For example, if a public A P I's spec is wrong, fix the OpenAPI file and create a test that asserts the A P I responses match the spec. That prevents the same drift from reoccurring. After recovery, schedule periodic lightweight reviews so rot cannot silently return. Which stale document in your project would you tackle first and why? content.html:
Warning › Documentation Rot
Symptoms & causes
  • Outdated examples or parameter lists.
  • Contradictory comments vs. code behavior.
  • Duplication across multiple documents.
Recovery steps
  1. Run triage and prioritize risky inaccuracies.
  2. Consolidate facts into an authoritative source and link others to it.
  3. Add tests or validation to prevent future drift.
Action

Start by fixing the documentation that, if incorrect, would cause a bug or broken integration for users. Use that fix to introduce a small validation test.

screens.title: Key Concepts

fullNarratorScript:
Documentation is a tool, not a trophy. In this lesson we'll adopt a pragmatic view: write what adds value, keep it close to the code when possible, and remove or refactor what becomes a liability. You will learn to apply the DRY principle to documentation, choose the right type of document for the job, and use living documentation so facts and behavior stay synchronized with code. We'll look at examples ranging from README files and lightweight docstrings to OpenAPI machine-readable specifications and executable specifications used as tests. I will also point out common traps that create documentation rot, and practical ways to recover a project that has accumulated stale artifacts. By the end you'll be able to judge whether a document should exist, where its single authoritative source should live, and how to keep it accurate with minimal ongoing cost. Think of documentation as ongoing code hygiene: do only what preserves clarity and reduces future friction. Which part of your next task could benefit most from a living document?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to make pragmatic decisions about when to create documentation and how to keep it accurate with minimal effort. You will articulate a philosophy of "just enough" and "just in time" documentation and identify the appropriate place for architectural notes, A P I specs, user guides, code comments, and READMEs. You will apply the DRY principle to documentation, ensuring each fact has a single authoritative home, and you will be able to convert static artifacts into living documentation when appropriate. Finally, you will recognize common pitfalls such as documentation rot and excessive, obvious commenting, and you will apply corrective strategies such as generating docs from code or turning requirements into executable specifications. These skills reduce maintenance overhead, improve onboarding, and preserve institutional knowledge. Picture deciding whether a team needs a short architecture note or a generated OpenAPI file and choosing the option that will stay accurate over time.

In addition to understanding the philosophy, you'll practice concrete habits that keep documentation healthy. You will write concise docstrings that describe why a function exists and highlight important constraints that cannot be expressed in the code alone. You will author a minimal README that helps a new contributor get the project running and find generated A P I docs. You will convert a static A P I description into a machine-readable OpenAPI spec and observe how that becomes living documentation. Finally, you'll perform a documentation triage exercise: evaluate existing artifacts, decide whether to refactor, replace with generated artifacts, or delete. These actions reduce friction and prevent documentation rot by keeping the authoritative facts close to the implementation and covered by tests where possible. Practicing these habits helps your team onboard faster and reduces bugs caused by outdated assumptions.

Pragmatic documentation is a deliberate practice: create only what helps someone understand or act, and store it where it will be maintained. This means distinguishing between information that is best expressed in code, and information that requires external prose. For example, naming a function clearly keeps its intended behavior visible; that is code-level documentation. High-level design decisions, trade-offs, or business rules often cannot be encoded directly and belong in a concise architectural note. The practical consequence is that every piece of information should have one authoritative home. Apply the DRY principle by avoiding duplicates across code comments, wikis, and long design documents. When duplication exists, divergence inevitably follows. A common misconception is that more documentation always reduces risk. In fact, excessive and redundant documentation increases risk because it becomes stale and misleading. A better habit is to write what is essential, keep it short, and treat documentation like code: review it, refactor it, and delete it when it is no longer useful. Consider the decision of whether to write a ten-page design doc or a one-page architecture note with an OpenAPI spec. The one-page note paired with an executable spec will usually be easier to maintain and more trustworthy. What single fact in your current project should move to a single authoritative source?

Applying DRY to documentation is a step-by-step process you can use on any project. First, identify facts that are repeated across code, comments, and external docs. These are the places where divergence will happen. Second, select the single authoritative home for each fact. If the fact is operational or A P I-shaped, put it in a machine-readable specification such as OpenAPI. If it is an implementation detail that is best expressed in code, prefer self-documenting names and minimal comments that explain intent, not mechanics. Third, remove duplicates and link to the authoritative source. Replace pasted examples with a small pointer or a generated snippet. Fourth, enforce the authority with automation: generate docs from the source, run tests that validate behavior, or include doc review in code review. A common mistake is to centralize the wrong thing — for example, placing high-level architectural rationale in auto-generated files where it will be lost. Keep rationale in human-authored notes and keep procedural facts in generated specs. As an exercise, take a README and a set of code comments, identify one duplicated claim, choose its authoritative source, and remove the other occurrences. How will your chosen authority be maintained going forward?

Different documentation types serve distinct audiences and purposes, and choosing the right one matters. Architectural documentation communicates high-level structure, major components, and design decisions. It is valuable for engineers making strategic changes and for new team members. A P I documentation describes how to interact with a service, often including endpoints, payload shapes, authentication, and error codes; when machine-readable it becomes living documentation. User documentation addresses end-user needs and is typically produced by product or documentation teams. Code comments should be used sparingly to explain why code exists or to note non-obvious constraints, not to restate the code's mechanics. A README is the project's front door: a short explanation, setup instructions, and a simple usage example. A common mistake is treating one long document as a catch-all. For example, burying A P I contract details inside a lengthy architecture doc reduces discoverability for A P I consumers. Instead, place each concern where the appropriate consumer will look and make links between them. To practice, pick a small project and list which facts belong in each document type and why. Docstrings and comments are often misused to state the obvious. The pragmatic rule is simple: prefer self-documenting code for the what, and use comments to explain intent, constraints, and rationale. Here are three compact ideas to remember. First, apply DRY to documentation: each fact should live in one authoritative place to avoid divergence. Second, prefer living documentation: when possible, make specs executable or generated from code so tests keep them truthful. Third, document intent not mechanics: write docstrings and architecture notes that explain why decisions exist, while keeping code readable enough to show what it does. These three concepts reduce maintenance, improve trust in documentation, and make onboarding smoother. Use these three quick checks when reviewing documentation. First, ask whether a fact has a single authoritative source and whether duplication can be removed. Second, verify whether important behaviors are expressed as executable specs or machine-readable contracts like OpenAPI. Third, examine comments and notes to ensure they explain rationale and assumptions rather than repeating the code. These checks fit naturally into pull request reviews and design sessions and help maintain trust in your project's documentation.
